newsitem.title: INDONESIA: ASEAN, Australia, NZ want WTO focus on trade.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN, Australia, NZ want WTO focus on trade.

text.p: Trade ministers from the ASEAN group and Australia and New Zealand agreed on Friday that the World Trade Organisation (WTO) meeting in Singapore in December should confine itself to core trade issues.
Australia's deputy prime minister and trade minister, Tim Fischer, said the WTO had been discussed in the annual talks between ASEAN, Australia and New Zealand.

"We agree with the ASEAN approach to stick to the core trade issues, and I would add particularly in relation to labour standards, which are best dealt with by the International Labour Organisation (ILO)...," Fischer told a news briefing.
"There was a great meeting of the minds on that," he said.
Asked if New Zealand agreed with this approach, minister for trade negotiations Philip Burdon replied: "Absolutely."

ASEAN members Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam strongly oppose the introduction of what they regard as extraneous issues such as labour standards, corruption, procurement and competition policies at the WTO's inaugural ministerial meeting.
The United States and some other Western nations have said they wanted such issues raised at Singapore.
Japan's minister of international trade and industry, Shunpei Tsukahara, who met separately with the ASEAN ministers, was more ambiguous when asked if he supported the ASEAN stand.

On the inclusion of labour standards, he said Japan saw the points of view of both sides, adding: "we should be cautious in dealing with this matter." Diplomatic sources, however, have said Japan also wanted the WTO to focus on core trade issues.

Indonesian coordinating minister of production and distribution, Hartarto, told reporters after the Australia-New Zealand meeting that the ministers had expressed concern at U.S. legislation that "imposes sanctions on countries or enterprises doing business with Cuba and several other countries."
The same formulation was used in a press statement following the ASEAN-Japan talks. Tsukahara said Japan had expressed its concern to Washington over the sanctions.
He said sanctions "could certainly raise problems of unilateralism that could be inconsistent with the WTO rules."
This was the second annual meeting of ASEAN with Australia and New Zealand, who are linked under the Closer Economic Relations trade agreement.

The ministers said the meeting had been very successful, and noted that total trade between the two regions had jumped to $15.8 billion in 1995 from $7.9 billion in 1990, and that ASEAN accounted for 14 percent of Australian-New Zealand exports.
All sides, including Japan, stressed the need to involve the private sector in the development process.
The ASEAN-Japan statement said the ministers "agreed on the importance of a conducive investment environment and the promotion of private sector investment in infrastructure."
The meetings followed two days of talks among the ASEAN ministers on progress in implementing the ASEAN Free Trade Area and other economic issues.
